text: Good evening, everyone. Welcome to the September 10th, 2026, meeting of the Audit Committee. I'm Anne Donahue. I'm the chair of this committee, and I apologize for being a few minutes late. I appreciate everyone's patience. With me are Mr. Pepper, the representative from the Dulles District, and Ms. Ricardi, the representative from the Sterling District. We will get started with the second item on our agenda, which is public comment.

Seeing that there are no sign-ups for public comment today, we will move straight into item number three on our agenda, which are minutes. The draft minutes from our August 5th, 2026, meeting were posted on BoardDocs prior to this meeting. Hopefully, my colleagues have had the opportunity to review the proposed draft. If there are any recommended or requested changes or edits, we can discuss those at this time. And otherwise, I will entertain a motion to approve. So moved.

Second. Thank you. That motion has been properly made by Ms. Ricardi and seconded by Mr. Pepper. All those in favor, please raise your hand and say aye. Aye. Aye. Abstain. I was not in attendance at the last meeting, so I will respectfully abstain. I should have maybe said if there is discussion. Okay, so Ms. Ricardi was a yes. I was a yes. So that motion does pass with two

board members in favor of the motion and with Mr. Pepper abstaining from the motion on the basis of his absence from the August 5th meeting. All right. Thank you. Then we will move on. Having no action items for today, we will move on to our one information item, the annual audit plan debrief. Mr. Woods, the floor is yours. Good evening, Madam Chair, members of the Audit Committee.

Tonight's presentation is a retrospective on the FY 2027 annual audit plan development process. Rather than discussing the audits themselves, the focus on this debrief is on the planning cycle that produced the approved 2027 audit plan. I'll walk you through how the audit universe was developed, how risk information was gathered and evaluated, what planning activities occurred after plan approval,

what lessons learned can be applied for the 2028 planning cycle. But most importantly, this discussion is intended to obtain your feedback, with the goal is continuous improvement of both the planning process and the information provided to the committee during future audit plan development. Next slide, please. This item is strictly for information. Today, I'm

not requesting the approval of any action or amendment to the audit plan at this point. As the governing body responsible for the oversight of the Office of the Auditor General, the Audit Committee plays a critical role in shaping the annual audit plan. Because of that oversight role, I believe it's important to periodically step back and assess not only what we chose to audit, but also how we arrived at those decisions. This debrief is intended to answer four questions.

Did the planning process function as intended? What worked well? What did we learn after detailed planning began? What should we change before developing the 2028 plan? The feedback received tonight will be incorporated into next year's universe development, risk assessment methodology, and plan selection process. Next slide.

The 2027 planning process began with a division-wide risk assessment. We gathered input from principals, senior staff, school board members, audit committee members, and observations from the broader DMV K-12 environment. That assessment helped identify and validate 38 audit topics across nine risk domains, establishing the 2027 audit universe.

From that universe, I developed and endorsed a list of 13 candidates for the committee's consideration. The endorsed list was then presented to the Audit Committee for discussion and selection. During those discussions, the committee identified an additional audit topic for consideration, which was the LCPS Sheriff's Office MOU sharing, which was subsequently approved and incorporated into the 2027 annual audit plan.

Following committee deliberations, a total of four were approved. One thing I'd like to point out is that the 38 topics were not simply a list of potential audits. They were the output of the OAG's annual risk assessment process and represented the areas where stakeholders, environmental factors, and professional judgment collectively identified organizational risk.

So even though only four audits were ultimately selected, every topic received documented consideration and risk evaluation during the audit planning. Next slide. After the committee approved the plan, a detailed planning began for each engagement. That planning produced a comprehensive risk and control matrix for all four audits. Across those four audits, we identified 88 individual risks.

Of those, 8 were assessed as critical, 33 as high, and 42 as moderate. And I want us to take a step back. And what this means is these are just questions that we'll potentially ask during the audit. These were not actual audits that were performed that identified these steps. These were general areas of risk identified just during the pre-planning of audits. And so when we do our audits, these are the questions we ask.

And so if you see employee reporting has two critical risks, it just means those are two areas during the audit process that we'll ask. It does not mean that those are two critical risk findings within the division. So look at this as 88 questions we will ask that we hope to gain, questions to those questions, during the audit. And we assess those questions as, is it a critical question?

Is it a high-risk question, or is it moderate? And so these are really just 88 questions we identified. And so I think that's a way to look at these identified risks for the audit planning. And so I think this tells an important story of the audit steps we will perform during those audits. The approved plan is not concentrated in a single area of organizational risk. Instead, it provides coverage across multiple risk domains.

For example, cybersecurity audit contains the largest concentration of elevated risk, including issues related to security monitoring, network architecture, vulnerability management, and incident detection capability. The federal grants audit contains significant compliance and financial stewardship risks, particularly around allowability of expenditures, documentation, monitoring, and reporting requirements.

For the sheriff's office information-sharing protocols, the risks are associated with FERPA compliance, law enforcement information sharing, threat assessment participation, and statutory notification requirements. One of the most significant risks identified within the audit involves timely reporting of reportable offenses to law enforcement. So during planning, that risk remained in the critical category, reflecting the

potential student safety and legal implications of delayed notification. For employee reporting and retaliation complaint oversight, two items were identified as high risk or critical risk profiles. They are employees may choose not to report concerns due to fear of retaliation, and the governance bodies may not receive sufficient reporting on complaint trends,

outcomes, and emerging concerns. Again, the way we look at this is these are questions we will ask during the audit. And so we do not know at this point if employees fear reporting out of fear of retaliation. Those are just the questions we are trying to ask and determine during the audit These risks are important because they can undermine management's visibility into

issues before they become larger organizational problems. Overall, the approved plan provides a mix of compliance, operational, governance, and cultural risk coverage. Next slide. So after looking at our planning process and the approval, I've assessed what I think went well. And looking back on the process, several elements worked

particularly well. First, multi-source risk assessment approach. Rather than relying on a single perspective, we incorporated viewpoints from principals, senior staff, board members, the committee, and environmental scan of the K12 risks. And so what that means is of those 38 topics that were in the audit universe, they were developed with input from principals, senior staff, board

members, and the committee. And so it really looks and incorporates the LCPS community when we developed those 38 topics. Second was documentation. Every major planning decision was supported by a written rationale that created transparency and traceability throughout the process. Third, planning work began aggressively and early.

Prior to fieldwork beginning, preliminary risk control matrixes, risk assessments, pre-audit surveys, and execution strategies have already been developed for all four audits. And so if you go back to the prior slide and saw those 88 identified critical risks, or not critical, but 88 identified risks, those have already began to be identified before we develop or before we get into the actual audits. And so we have performed some pre-planning ahead of execution of

those audits. Finally, committee engagement was meaningful. The final approved plan reflects committee deliberation and discussion. It was not simply a staff-generated plan presented for approval without modification. So in my view, those are all positive indicators of a maturing audit planning process. Next slide, please.

Once detailed planning began, several important observations emerged. The first was that planning successfully identified capability gaps before fieldwork started. Specifically, portions of the cybersecurity audit involved highly specialized areas such as security monitoring, effectiveness, and network architecture evaluation. And so cybersecurity had eight identified

risks. Out of those 26, two of them are the OAG office has capability gaps. And so those two particular items, we will not be able to perform in-house. And so in order to resolve those, we'll have to have audit committee discussion. Also, there may be mitigating factors in that

DDI or IT department may already receive outside expertise in those areas, which we'll dig into once we perform the audit. But out of those 26 areas that are risk-based, two of them we do not have the internal expertise to perform. And again, those would be needed for IT experts to look at that. And so those items were identified prior to performing the audit.

And personally, I think that is part of the process and a good practice. So planning exists partly to identify resource constraints before audit execution when corrective action is still possible. Second, planning highlighted the impact of mandatory topical requirements or mandatory professional requirements. As we map the cybersecurity audit, IIA, or Institute of Internal Auditors,

has topical requirements that were applicable to that audit, and that expanded the scope to include additional risks that had not been identified during the universe stage. Again, this is a normal process and expected outcome of planning. Third, we learned an important lesson regarding complexity versus risk. A highly complex audit is not necessarily the highest audit risk. Likewise, a relatively straightforward audit may address some of the most

significant risks facing the organization. So going forward, I believe separating complexity from risk more explicitly will improve committee decision-making. Next slide, please. After planning activities were completed, I looked at the plan against our office capacity. We currently have three staff available for fieldwork execution.

I evaluated three potential models. A fully sequential approach would have us working on one audit at a time, and would be the least efficient. And so after we complete one audit, we'd start another audit and just doing preliminary planning. Doing it that way, we believe that our plan would be completed until December 2027. Instead, we like a fully parallel approach.

And so what that looks like is starting an audit, most likely every six to eight weeks during the fiscal year. So we'll start the LCPS chairs office audit first, which began this week. And then in six to eight weeks, we'll start a second audit. And from there on, the operational plan is to follow the same cadence of every six to eight weeks for these four audits is to begin a new audit. So they'll go parallel.

Under that approach, all four audits are projected to be completed sometime in spring 2027, leaving approximately a few weeks of contingency before fiscal year end. Based on prior planning assumptions, it's my assessment that the approved plan is achievable. Next slide, please. During the audit plan approval, there was discussion regarding whether audits should be added.

So right now we have four. In prior discussions in the audit committee, we discussed adding four to five, and in the last meeting, we talked about possibly adding them today. I recommend waiting until November before making that decision, for three particular reasons. First, we have not began fieldwork on any of those audits. And so, because we haven't generated any meaningful data, we just don't know how long it

will be to analyze that data. So that's one of the reasons to wait till November. Second, the current schedule is already sequenced. And third, capability questions associated with portions of the cybersecurity audit have not yet been fully resolved. And so before adding work, I believe we should determine where we are in that audit process for those audits that were

approved. So rather than deciding today when to add more audits, I propose providing the committee with a formal capacity assessment in November, based on actual engagement process. And if capacity exists at that time, to provide new audit topics that can be approved in December. And so that is what I propose we do as opposed to adding new topics today. Next slide, please.

Planning also identified several opportunities to strengthen future cycles for universe development. Increase survey participation. We surveyed all principals. We received 31. I don't control who responds, but I do think if we engage them earlier, then maybe we can increase participation. And so giving them more time to respond, it

helps suit their busy schedules to give them more time to review it and adequately address those surveys. For the risk assessment, apply formal likelihood and impact scoring sooner. And so what that looks like is if we have an audit universe, we apply a likelihood and an impact of the audit topics, which is a risk practice. And so you'll see an audit topic and its associated likelihood and impact.

Now again, these are preliminary assessments, and we really truly get to a finalized risk until the end of the audit. But I do believe providing that to the audit committee in earlier stages helps with the approval process, and it helps you be more informed when looking at the audit universe. utilisezrandootu imggel cou Un �

the critical, high, moderate risk assessment and what those designations mean? Yes. So we look at the likelihood of an event occurring, and then what's its impact. So if the likelihood is assessed at one and the impact is 10, so it's an event that would not happen very often,

but if it were to happen, it would create such an impact that it would have a critical negative impact on LCPS operations, then it is considered critical. If it has a assessed likelihood of three and impact of three, and I'm just going to use this on a 1 to 10 scale, that's around a six, that's a moderate or high. I would give six a high

assessment. And so it's what is the likelihood of an event occurring, and what is the impact of an event.
